column3: The identical great-day punishment is framed as the messenger's fear for his own disobedience, a close but different stance from Hud's protective fear for his people.
Its inescapable recompense for what people did gives the punitive-day horizon behind Hud's warning a direct outcome.
The greatness of final success does not clarify Hud's fear for his people of punishment.
It repeats the great-day punishment but locates fear in the messenger's own possible disobedience rather than concern for a community.
The immediate response treats Hud's warning as immaterial whether or not he admonishes, directly displaying the denial his fear confronts.
Fear of a grim day motivates present conduct, paralleling the forward-looking caution in Hud's warning without its communal address or punishment formula.
Nuh likewise tells his people that he fears for them punishment on a day, closely matching Hud's protective prophetic warning.
The rejection of a warner from among the people explains the reception-side resistance that makes Hud's warning urgent.
Fear of a day whose evil spreads outward turns into faithful action, strongly paralleling the warning's call to avert a future harm.
The believer says explicitly that he fears for his people a punishing historical day, closely reproducing Hud's protective address.
The immediate Hud conclusion joins their denial to destruction, supplying the realized consequence anticipated in the focus.
Its great report shares the language of magnitude but does not specify a protective warning or punitive day.
The repeated phrase "I fear for you" and a named future day make this a close prophetic counterpart to Hud's warning.
Prior communities offered as admonition give a direct instructional framework for the warning Hud delivers.
Concern for vulnerable descendants is protective fear, but it concerns social responsibility rather than divine punishment.
Nuh's address is an exact parallel: a messenger fears for his people punishment on a tremendous day.
Pharaoh's description of a small group does not clarify Hud's warning of punishment.
The phrase "great deviation" concerns moral inclination, not the tremendous punitive day feared for Hud's people.
The warning of the brother of Ad repeats the focus wording exactly and gives the same protective prophetic stance.
The stories of messengers are expressly made warning and reminder, framing prior prophetic accounts as caution for later hearers.
An appointed day that cannot be advanced or delayed strengthens the fixed, unavoidable horizon of the warned punishment.
It repeats fear of the great-day punishment for personal disobedience, closely related but not the communal concern voiced by Hud.
The statement about inserting the revelation into criminals' hearts does not develop Hud's fear or the punitive day.
A great share granted to the patient is a distinct use of greatness and offers no warning-of-punishment connection.
Punishment explicitly called the punishment of a tremendous day gives a direct narrative realization of the formula Hud fears for his people.
A father's warning against grave wrongdoing supplies a close ethical model of protective counsel, though its "great" quality is not a day of punishment.
Freedom from fear for God's allies is a broad positive counterpart, without the prophetic warning or day of punishment.
The conditional warning that wrongdoing will bring punishment on a tremendous day closely matches the focus's threatened outcome.
Refusing to expel believers does not clarify the warning or its punitive horizon.
Great character is unrelated to fear for a people of a great day.
The compact phrase "for a tremendous day" directly names the eschatological scale of the day Hud invokes.
Calling incoming truth false supplies the denial pattern that the Hud narrative connects to ruin.
Revering divine rites links greatness with piety, but not with the threatened day or a messenger's protective fear.
Musa's fear that he will be called a liar provides a same-surah prophetic pressure parallel, though not a fear for others of punishment.
The provision of food and drink does not clarify Hud's warning.
The day that overturns even closest family relations gives concrete gravity to the great day Hud fears for his people.
A messenger says directly that he fears for his people punishment on a great day if they turn away, a close wording and function parallel.
Nuh's ineffective counsel and return to God extend the warning-and-response setting shared by Hud's address.
Great success after deliverance does not add to the warning of punishment.
Shuayb explicitly fears for his people an encompassing day of punishment, closely matching Hud's protective prophetic concern.
Creation and guidance do not clarify the threatened day.
Righteous response removes fear and grief, offering only a general positive alternative to the danger Hud announces.
Abraham's fear that punishment will touch his father is a direct instance of protective warning for another person.
The divine admonition to Nuh belongs to the counsel-and-warning frame, but it does not name Hud's communal fear or great day.
A remaining sign serves those who fear painful punishment, showing past destruction functioning as the caution Hud seeks to evoke.
The promise of no fear on the day gives a broad salvific counterpart to the future danger in Hud's warning.
Pharaoh's threat against the magicians is not connected to Hud's warned divine punishment.
A great report shares magnitude language but does not develop the fear-for-a-people or punishment relation.
Musa's fear of being called a liar parallels a prophet's anticipation of rejection, though its object is not a punitive day for the people.
The conditional promise of charity does not clarify the warning or its consequence.
The Day of Resurrection as an eventual exposure gives a remote future-day context without Hud's warning of punishment.
Pharaoh invokes fear to justify killing Musa, the opposite of Hud's protective warning against divine punishment.
Wisdom and gratitude do not clarify the great punitive day.
Musa's personal vigilance under threat is a different, individual form of fear from Hud's concern for his people.
Fear of God prevents retaliatory killing, supplying an ethical consequence of rightly directed fear rather than Hud's announced punishment.
Woe for the deniers gives the concise punitive result toward which Hud's rejected warning points.
The greatness of an oath has no direct connection to a tremendous day of punishment.
It explicitly joins fear of afterlife punishment with a day when all people are gathered and witnessed, directly expanding Hud's threatened day.
The repeated woe for deniers again gives the punitive consequence of refusing a warning.
Questioning the timing of the Day of Recompense reflects resistance to the future accountability Hud invokes.
It contrasts misplaced fear of associates with the fear warranted by associating partners with God, clarifying the moral direction of fear.
The command to fear God rather than hostile allies gives a general norm for rightly locating fear, though not Hud's day-of-punishment warning.
Satan claims to fear God when abandoning his followers, a distorted fear scene only distantly related to Hud's sincere protective concern.
Musa's fear of retaliation is a concrete prophetic danger that parallels the vulnerability of a messenger, not the communal punishment Hud foresees.
Satan's claim to fear God is exposed as abandonment after inciting disbelief, contrasting with Hud's protective warning.
Entering the Fire on the Day of Recompense makes the punitive character of the warned day explicit.
A great punishment for harmful speech supplies a direct divine-punishment pattern, though not the particular day Hud names.
Universal surrender on that day gestures toward final judgment but adds little about the warning or its cause.
The declaration of great punishment gives a general consequence for persistent rejection, supporting the horizon of Hud's warning.
The reiterated question about the Day of Recompense emphasizes the exceptional gravity of the day Hud calls tremendous.
Great punishment following division after clear proofs gives a broader precedent for punishment after rejecting guidance.
The magnified reward for piety does not clarify the feared punishment day.
A great throne is unrelated to Hud's warning.
The postponement of messengers to a designated day supports the fixed temporal horizon of judgment.
After judgment is settled, Satan's abandonment and the punishment of wrongdoers show the final consequence of following false calls rather than warning.
A known appointed day supplies only a general temporal parallel to Hud's tremendous day.
Fear, worldly disgrace, and great afterlife punishment follow violating sacred space, giving a broad warning-and-consequence pattern.
The great throne concerns divine sovereignty, not the threatened punishment day.
Even those invoked besides God seek their Lord's mercy and fear His punishment, directly affirming that this punishment is to be heeded.
The request for delay until resurrection is a temporal link only, without a protective warning or punishment description.
Not fearing the Hereafter identifies the inner refusal that renders warnings like Hud's ineffective.
Reassurance that Musa need not fear concerns rescue from a hostile people, not the divine day Hud announces.
Fear of God in the unseen is tested by conduct, and transgression receives painful punishment, a related accountability frame.
The reassurance to Lot distinguishes future fear from grief but does not develop Hud's warning of a great day.
No fear or grief for faithful, righteous people gives a broad positive counterpart to the danger of punishment.
The Day of Decision explicitly names the judgment function implicit in Hud's tremendous day.
The removal of fear for faithful communities is only a general counterpart to the threatened punishment.
Denying the Day of Recompense directly names the rejection of future accountability that Hud's warning addresses.
Fear of a day that overturns hearts and sight gives a concrete experiential portrait of the tremendous day Hud fears for his people.
Hope in God and the Last Day is a broad positive orientation, not a warning of punishment.
A prophetic prohibition backed by near punishment closely resembles Hud's warning structure, though it does not name a tremendous day.
A known public day in the same surah has no punitive or warning function comparable to the focus.
Those striving against the signs receive painful punishment, supplying a general consequence for opposition to divine warning.
Those left in denial will meet the day on which they are struck down, directly portraying the feared punitive encounter.
The announcement of divine forgiveness and mercy offers only a partial counterbalance, without the accompanying warning of punishment.
Hope in the Last Day is joined to refraining from corruption, a positive temporal orientation that contrasts with the path toward punishment.
Abraham's departure toward his Lord does not clarify Hud's warning.
Fear and hope before natural signs are a distinct response pattern, not fear for a people of a punitive day.
The command to fear God while observing a legal waiting term gives only a remote norm of accountability.
Abraham refuses fear of false associates while acknowledging God's encompassing will, clarifying the distinction between misplaced fear and fear grounded in God.
Ad's denial of the messengers begins the immediate narrative sequence in which Hud's warning is rejected and fulfilled.
Hud's immediate question, "Will you not fear?", supplies the ethical summons that his fear-for-them warning seeks to awaken.
Hud's declaration that he is a trustworthy messenger establishes the protective authority from which the warning is issued.
The command to fear God and obey Hud gives the direct response that would avert the punishment he fears for them.
Hud's refusal of payment supports the disinterested character of his counsel but does not itself develop the punitive day.
The rebuke for building conspicuous structures on every height directly frames the focus reading's contrast between material grandeur and the greater coming day.
Their construction of fortresses as though they would live forever sharply opposes the mortality and judgment horizon of the tremendous day.
Striking others like tyrants gives the community's violent conduct that stands under Hud's warning of punishment.
The renewed command to fear God and obey Hud immediately precedes and interprets his protective fear for the people.
The reminder of God's provisions shows the gifts whose misuse and ingratitude make the warning consequential.
The enumeration of livestock and children continues the reminder of entrusted abundance before the threatened punishment.
Gardens and springs complete the catalogue of prosperity that the community wrongly treats as secure against the coming day.
Calling Hud's message merely an ancient custom is the immediate dismissal that explains why his warning is not heeded.
Their assertion that they will not be punished directly contradicts the very punishment Hud fears for them.
The closing affirmation of divine might and mercy frames the authority and mercy of the warning after Ad's destruction.
Hud's commission to Ad establishes the same prophetic address and call to exclusive worship underlying the warning in 26:135.
The chiefs' charge that Hud is foolish gives a close reception-side parallel to the community's dismissal of his warning.
Hud rejects the charge and identifies himself as a messenger from the Lord, grounding his warning in delegated authority.
Hud says he conveys his Lord's messages and gives faithful counsel, directly characterizing the protective purpose of his fear for Ad.
The reminder that Ad was increased in bodily stature and strength closely complements the focus reading's contrast of great human structures with a greater day.
Ad's objection to abandoning inherited worship shows the resistant posture that receives Hud's warning as a threat to established practice.
Hud announces that punishment and wrath have become due and calls them to wait, directly advancing the punishment foreseen in the focus.
The rescue of Hud and destruction of those denying the signs gives the realized outcome of the warning.
Hud's address to Ad as a messenger calling them to worship God supplies the same mission setting as the focus.
Hud's refusal of payment confirms sincere counsel but adds little beyond the immediate parallel in 26:127.
The call to seek forgiveness and return gives a concrete path away from the punishment Hud warns of.
Ad's refusal to abandon their gods records the defiant response to Hud's prophetic warning.
Their accusation that Hud has been harmed by their gods is a rejection detail with limited direct bearing on the punitive day.
Hud's trust in the Lord who holds every creature denies Ad any autonomous power against the divine judgment he announces.
Hud warns that turning away will bring replacement, extending the consequence of refusing his message.
God's rescue of Hud and the believers from a severe punishment supplies the deliverance counterpart to Ad's threatened fate.
It identifies Ad as rejecting their Lord's signs and following every stubborn tyrant, directly naming the conduct that the Hud passage condemns before warning of punishment.
The curse in this world and the Day of Resurrection gives Ad's rejection a lasting judgment horizon.
Ad demand that Hud bring the punishment he promises, directly reenacting their refusal to take his warning seriously.
Hud answers that knowledge of the timing belongs to God and that he only conveys the message, clarifying the messenger's warning role.
The cloud they mistake for rain is identified as the painful punishment they had demanded, directly realizing the threatened day.
The destructive wind leaves Ad's dwellings desolate, giving the concrete consequence of their rejected warning.
Their exceptional power and faculties fail to protect them when they deny God's signs, extending the focus contrast between worldly greatness and divine punishment.
Ad's boast that none is stronger than they are directly exposes the false confidence in human magnitude that Hud's tremendous day overturns.
The sending of a humiliating wind and its lasting punishment gives another direct account of Ad's threatened consequence.
Ad's denial begins a compact retelling of the same people whose rejection of warning ends in destruction.
The relentless wind sent on an evil day gives a direct punitive-day realization for Ad.
The wind's violent removal of people concretely portrays the overwhelming consequence of their denial.
The refrain asking how warning and punishment proved true reinforces the vindication of Hud's warning.
Ad's destruction by a furious, violent wind is a direct account of the punishment feared for them.
The wind's sustained devastation gives the scale and finality appropriate to the tremendous day announced by Hud.
The question whether any remnant remains records the total consequence of Ad's refusal.
The explicit naming of Ad anchors the passage's monumental imagery to the people addressed by Hud.
Iram of the lofty pillars directly reinforces the focus reading's contrast between imposing built grandeur and the greater divine reckoning.
Its unparalleled construction or like in the lands makes human exceptionalism the very backdrop that the coming punishment disproves.
The destruction of the former Ad supplies a concise retrospective confirmation of the danger Hud warned against.
